Legionbound offers up a solid auto-battler experience while giving the player freedom to be as involved (or not) in decision making during a run. You can micromanage your team, controlling where every gold piece is spent. Or, you can enable "Idle Mode" after you've played a bit. Then, you can automate every action (except for optimal battlefield positioning, which is up to you to do). As a result of this freedom, you kinda have 2 games here. One, an auto-battler that allows for deep customization and a TON of opportunities to min/max and squeeze every last stat. The other, ez mode just kicking back and watching the chaos unfold. There is a medium-sized skill tree that you will fill out pretty quickly. There are 3 special nodes that you can pick at any 1 time. These are keystone passive skills that tailor the fights to your style. If you have ever played Path of Exile you have some idea of what it looks like. Just whittle that tree's size down a bit. But the concept is similar. Some examples of keystones available: +Phys dmg at expense of Magic dmg; 25% cheaper upgrades; Ultimate charges faster; Magic attacks have chance to duplicate.... etc..... You get the idea. One word of caution, though: this genre doesn't play well with the 2 hour refund window. You really don't get a solid idea of the game till after that. Considering time is needed for everything to play out, you will find yourself over 2 hours before you know it. So, maybe watch some Youtube vids with gameplay just to be sure. Have fun and I'll see ya'll next time! Koma-OUT!

This is such a close one for me between yes and no. Also important note, it does run great on steam deck with the little trackpad. All of my time playing is on steam deck and i've had no issues. The real problem is that you just get everything every run. It needs more limitations. They leaned really hard into the "screen exploding" side which is fun, but they pushed it too far. In vampire survivors or ballxpit you get a limited number of weapons and the trick is how you get the screen to explode with just a few of the things. In this you literally have more "slots" than you do "weapons". In this you build an army to do auto-battle which is a ton of fun and a really neat take. But your recruit pool is all of the things that have been unlocked, so you just get everything every time. There are no builds, you can just hit auto-buy on everything and it will play itself very comfortably once you have a little meta-progression. The idea is so good. But in order to have replay value and interesting builds it needs to lean into more restrictions and depth of interactions instead of just 50 GUYS GO BRRRRR. That kind of unbalanced insanity is fun initially but goes stale so fast.

I hate games that lock everything behind repeated dying. You die. You gain gems. You need them to unlock power trees. You die. You unlock characters that give you synergies. So you simply get a little bit further with each death because the game is handholding you to the next slightly higher level of power. Meanwhile, you basically just watch everything play out while adding stuff to your roster based on the unlocks youved died over and over again. I honestly hate this S***. I hate the game recipe of making an incredibly simple game and the only thing essentially keeping you from progressing is you haven't grinded enough deaths yet. It creates the illusional of progression and complexity when it doesn't really exists. It's literally just grinding deaths for one just a little more power to get a little futher next time. It's cute for a couple hours til you realize what's going on and then it's BORING!

the game feels for the most part by far too simplisitc, with a lot of it's time being due to grinding time gates and obfuscating numbers. like dexterity increased... evasion, crit chance, accuracy? by how much? no idea. what do these levels do? no idea. just some obscure numbers. str increases atk dam. mag increases magic dam. by how much? 1 for 1 point? do certain skills have better ratios, is it always 1 for 1? how much do the stat growths actually matter? what do they mean? your char has an ultimate which shoots people. how many? how much damage? is it basic damage? no idea!! no idea. and these decisions probably don't matter cause in the grand scheme the game is too simple for it to actually matter. just vibes your way to victory by spamming stuff that feels like its doing something. you want to see what these stats even attempt to do? hovering over them doesnt work, instead u have to enter the glossary and scroll to find out. why cant it just display the number? idk. maybe cause it's actually wrong and we'd know? who knows if something is bugged if u just cant tell the numbers. why does changing the stupid zoom on ultimate, or screenshake involve hitting apply settings. then closing that menu and hit apply settings again in the bigger menu. why do i have to apply my settings twice, why not once. it's in the end an insignificant thing but kinda shows a lack of polish and clarity in how the game was made. the skill tree being a bunch of small dots ontop of a background that's also a bunch of small dots was certainly a decision of all time. i enjoy the poe tree but this one is just there for the sake of being there. the nodes increasing in size a little bit when u zoom out would be a great change. a lot of the games longevity is just unlocking stuff and discovering what it does, not the actual gameplay. you get thrown everything at you in a single run that things aren't different enough. my 3 runs were legitimately doing the same thing repeatedly except cause more meta progression i got a bit further and my numbers got bigger till i eventually lost. the synergy system imo forces the game into being played in certain ways, you just rainbow your board with "this makes this synergy better" of whatever unit u found to be useful. idk there's a lot of flash, the game doesn't like to tell u things, and the gametime is delayed by progression. does not feel like there is a lot of game here. just vibes with funny colours as ur not rly allowed to do much else.

I don't really know how to review this one. Like, [i]technically[/i] the game is what it says on the tin- there are class synergies, there is a party based RPG dynamic, there is some amount of choice you're making. But, this is an idle game through and through. Sure, you do make a one time decision on where to place a unit, but typically you aren't moving them once placed. Sure, when you're first starting to play you want to maximize aura buffs by centering heroes around someone, but that falls away pretty quickly once you develop meta progression and are just, well, [b]idling[/b]. Because that's what all the choices boil away to show in the end- that this is an idle game and the difference between selecting units, items, and placement compared to what the computer will do for you in the idle mode is really no different. A lot of the choices in the game are illusions of choice. Yeah, you want your defense units in the front and your squishies in the back. Duh. That's not really making a meaningful choice, that's just the fact that squishies will die if they get hit. And, yeah, you want to take X unit with Y unit because they synergize, and you can only get more powerful units (ascended units) if you syngerize them. None of this is really choice. Choice implies that there's a second option that is equally valid, and in this game there's none of that. You get the choice of what you want to focus on in the sense of excluding certain units from your team, but there's not really a huge amount of variability here. Do you want to focus on Dex, Str, or Mag units? Cool, focus on that type and then splash Def units for frontline shielding. There. That's the biggest choice you'll make. They all play relatively the same. You just pick the keystones from the meta progression that benefit the type of units you're focusing on and you're done. And you are done. I've found that the idle mode plays the game better than I can as it will instantly buy new units, which at the highest speed is the limiting factor. A boss suddenly kills two front liners? No biggie, the computer just bought two new units to replace them so the attacks don't start cascading into your backrow causing even more losses; for a person, by the time a message pops up alerting you of a dead unit, three more are already dead and now you're struggling to salvage what remains. There is an adventure mode, which is like a drafting rouglike? You can build areas that give you specific bonuses and give you the ability to purchase specific units, all while you climb up progressively more difficult waves of enemies to a final boss. I personally found it really tedious. What little enjoyment I got out of watching my team destroy wave after wave of enemies was dragged down by the constant line of "choices" and up-keeping you had to make after a few waves. It felt less like a rougelike and more like a very tedious idle game. And this is where I don't know how to review the game. It doesn't really succeed at being an auto-battler as your choices aren't that impactful. It doesn't really succeed as a rougelike either as each run will look nearly identical once you find your niche. And it doesn't really succeed as an idler as you do have to check on it somewhat frequently just to see if you've lost with zero interactability outside of that. After playing it for ten hours, I was bored. I had seen everything and wasn't truly that impressed or interested. Overall, the game does play well and, as far as I know, I didn't encounter any bugs- although, when the game is whipping past you at top speed, it's hard to say if a bug actually happens. I just can't recommend this- at least not at full price. I think for $4 it's worth a play, but anything more than that is not great. This is an idle game, an idle game that tries to cloak itself in something else, but still just an idle game. If I want to [i]not[/i] play a game, I'll just go knit while watching someone else play something.

First off: Don't write this game off as another idle clicker. It's not. It's an auto-battler & party management game, where planning and bit of foresight goes a long way. Yes you can automate certain things, and eventually you can unlock Idle Mode (with good customization options), but I can't bring myself to call it idle clicker. Planning and preparation are both important factors, you don't just mash your mouse button and hit "Upgrade" button every now and then. Most of the decision making and player input comes in the shopping screen and arranging your party members, and for the most part battle is automated. You do get to cast spells as you buy them, some of them being useful (Frost Nova and Confusion) and some less so. You can also pause the game and re-arrange party members positions if necessary. It's really not a zero-input idle game. You've got Adventure Mode for roguelike experience, Battle Mode and Endless Mode (Basically same as Battle, except... endless, surprisingly). Overall a solid 8/10. Wish there was more to explore in Adventure Mode, but it's good as it is.

Legionbound is a genuinely cool idea that never closes the gap between concept and execution. Once you've cleared the early unlocks, the core loop stops being a game and starts being something that wants to be a screensaver — but never lets you treat it like one. You'd think enough progress would let you sit back, but you can't: gold and gems have to be manually picked up, so you're constantly waving your cursor around the screen chasing loot, and shop purchases run on a timer you have to babysit even though the queue just buys whatever's available with no way to target a specific need. It's not idle and it's not actively directed either — it's a third thing, a chore that borrows the worst of both. The talent tree makes this worse instead of better. Under-invested, progress is nearly impossible; past a certain threshold, everything becomes trivial. There's no middle where the tree is actually shaping meaningful decisions — it's a wall, then a light switch. Ascensions, which look like the game's most interesting mechanic, are gated tightly enough that you never get a real feel for their impact before you're pushed back into the grind. And the build space overall skews hard toward stacking raw damage; other combinations exist but don't seem viable for continued progress, so experimentation gets punished rather than rewarded. I put 11 hours into it — genuinely locked in the whole time. Stepping back, I have no pull to return. If you're looking for a casual auto-battler, you'll enjoy this. But if you're looking for something deeper, you'll probably find this one too grindy.
